title: Ngondro, the foundations
hookLine: the preliminary practices: refuge and prostration, purification, offering, guru yoga

lines: WITHOUT ONE, THE HOUSE TELLS YOU.
cards: Nobody stops on the sidewalk to admire a foundation. It's poured first, it's underground, and soon it's covered with floors and furniture. But build a house without one and the house will tell you.
Doors stick. Cracks run up the walls. Tibetan Buddhism has a name for the work that goes under everything else, the part nobody photographs and some practitioners spend years on.
Yesterday's bow was the first piece of it. Today's word is the whole foundation: ngondro.

teach.b: First, the word. Ngondro is Tibetan, usually translated the preliminaries: the practices that come before the deeper meditations a teacher may give later. But before doesn't mean less.
Refuge and prostration: going to the Buddha, the teaching and the community, with the body bowing all the way down. Purification: the mantra of Vajrasattva, for washing away past wrongs.

The mandala offering: giving away the whole world, pictured on a plate of rice. And guru yoga: joining your mind with the teacher's awakened mind. Each gets its own day this week; today is just the map.

In some lineages the ngondro opens with four thoughts that turn the mind, the same four that opened mind training last week: the preciousness of a human life, impermanence, karma, and the suffering of the round.
Other schools arrange their preliminaries in their own order, with their own lists.
Tradition sets each practice at a large number of repetitions, and people often complete them slowly, around jobs and families, over a long time. Fourth, why the foundation matters so much.

A saying heard in Tibetan teaching puts it boldly: the preliminaries are more profound than the main practice. Some teachers go back to them again and again, long after finishing. A foundation isn't the part you outgrow.
It's the part everything else stands on.

how: Tibetan Buddhist students complete the ngondro under a teacher's guidance, doing refuge with prostrations, Vajrasattva purification, the mandala offering and guru yoga, often over years and alongside ordinary life.

o: the vows a monk takes on entering a monastery
an easy beginner stage that serious students skip
the preliminaries: foundational practices that come first

p: the body bowing to the three jewels
the whole world on a plate of rice

s: ngondro is only for beginners, then left behind
a saying in Tibetan teaching calls the preliminaries more profound than the main practice; some go back to them for life.

along with refuge and prostration, and guru yoga.

games.q: you've finished the preliminaries after years of steady work. a teacher you trust says something about them. what is it likely to be?
o: good, now you can forget them.
the preliminaries are more profound than the main practice.
games.why: a saying in Tibetan teaching puts it that way, and some teachers return to the foundations again and again.

practice: Picture a plain square slab of foundation, seen from above, and set one practice at each corner as you breathe: refuge and prostration, purification, the offering, guru yoga.

Walk around the square once more, slower, letting each one sit for a moment; you don't need to do any of them, just know where each one stands. Then rest in the plain breath under it, the way a house rests on what's underneath.

wordCard.voice: Ngondro. The preliminaries, the foundations of Tibetan practice: refuge and prostration, purification, offering, guru yoga. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan ngondro: the preliminaries, the practices that come before.

carryVoice: Your line: the foundations are never outgrown. Ngondro: quiet work, poured first, and holding up everything else. Until tomorrow.
